questions.q: Per Salesforce's own Large Data Volumes guidance, roughly what scale of deployment is flagged as a real architectural concern?
options: Tens of thousands of users, tens of millions of records, or hundreds of gigabytes of record storage
Any org with more than 1,000 total records
Only orgs using more than one Salesforce license type
Only orgs that use Big Objects
questions.explain: Salesforce's Large Data Volumes guidance names this rough threshold — tens of thousands of users, tens of millions of records, or hundreds of GB of storage — as the point where data structure and operations can change performance by orders of magnitude.

questions.q: What happens when an Apex transaction exceeds a governor limit, such as issuing more than the allowed number of SOQL queries?
options: The transaction slows down but still completes successfully
Salesforce silently skips the extra queries
The transaction throws a runtime exception and fails outright
The limit is automatically raised for that transaction
questions.explain: Governor limits are hard caps — exceeding one throws a runtime exception and the transaction fails, which is why a data model that risks exceeding limits as volume grows is a design defect, not a tunable slowdown.

questions.q: Why does filtering a SOQL query on an indexed field matter more as an object's record count grows into the millions?
options: Indexed fields let the query optimizer avoid an expensive full-table scan, which matters enormously at high volume
Indexed fields are required before any SOQL query can run at all
Indexing has no effect on SOQL query performance
Only custom objects support field indexing
questions.explain: A selective query that filters on an indexed field avoids a full-table scan — a cost that barely matters on a small object but becomes very significant once the object holds millions of rows.

questions.q: What is bulkification, and why does it matter for scalability?
options: Writing automation to process records in batches rather than one at a time, so governor-limit cost doesn't multiply per record processed one-by-one
Increasing the org's total data storage allocation
A Salesforce feature that automatically archives old records
Disabling triggers entirely for large data loads
questions.explain: Automation that processes records one at a time multiplies every governor-limit cost by the number of records in the transaction; bulkified automation handles a batch in a single pass, keeping limit usage proportional to the work, not the record count.

questions.q: According to the Large Data Volumes guidance's core point, when should scalability be designed in?
options: After launch, once performance problems actually appear in production
Only if the org exceeds its storage limit
During the design phase, before the schema and automation are built, since retrofitting is far more expensive and risks production failures in the interim
Scalability does not need to be designed for on the Salesforce platform
questions.explain: The guidance's central point is that design-phase decisions (selectivity, bulkification, skew avoidance, archiving) are far cheaper to build in from the start than to retrofit after volume has already grown and governor-limit failures have started appearing in production.
